issues.legal_issue: A grantee whose land is taken through statutory acquisition is entitled to compensation for the grantee’s interest, valued subject to a restriction reserved to the government in the grant.
material_facts: The government granted land subject to a condition requiring the grantees to surrender it without compensation if the government required it.
The government acquired the land through the statutory process, took possession under its urgency power, and did not invoke the grant condition to obtain the land.
The acquisition officer awarded no compensation for the land, though compensation was awarded for improvements.
issues.conclusion: After taking possession under statutory authority, the government could not resort to the grant condition to avoid compensation. The grantees were entitled to compensation for their interest, measured by the market value of that interest subject to the government’s reserved right.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 4 and 17 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the government may acquire land for a public purpose and, in an urgent case, take possession so that the land vests in it. As reflected in Attorney-General v. De Keyser’s Royal Hotel Ltd., the government cannot obtain possession under statutory authority and then rely on a different source of power to avoid the consequences of that statutory process. But the restriction in the grant remains relevant to valuation: compensation is the market value, at the date of notification, of the interest actually held by the grantee, subject to that restriction.

predicates.statutory_land_acquisition_case: The government acquired the land through a statutory land-acquisition proceeding.
predicates.government_took_possession_under_acquisi: The government took possession of the land under the statutory acquisition process.
predicates.grant_restricted_grantee_interest: The grant gave the grantee an interest in the land subject to a government right that restricted the grantee’s rights.

issues.definition: When land is taken in a statutory acquisition proceeding and the grantee’s rights were restricted by a government right in the grant, the grantee receives the market value of the restricted interest.

issues.legal_issue: A government may assert its interest or a restrictive right in land during acquisition proceedings, and the acquisition may extend to the private interests outstanding in the land.
material_facts: The grant reserved to the government a right requiring surrender of the land without compensation if the government required it.
The government acquired the land through the statutory process rather than exercising the right reserved in the grant.
The acquisition officer treated the grantees as entitled to no compensation for the land, while the High Court directed that compensation be determined.
issues.conclusion: The government was not estopped from asserting its interest or restrictive right in the acquisition proceeding. The statutory process could be applied to acquire the private interests outstanding in the land, with compensation limited to the market value of those interests subject to the government’s right.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(a) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 defines land to include benefits arising out of land and things attached to the earth. Although the Act is silent on acquiring partial interests, that silence does not exclude acquisition of an interest restricted by a government right. Compensation is apportioned among those entitled to the interests acquired, and a private interest subject to a government right is valued subject to that right. The Court followed Government of Bombay v. Esufali Salebhai and approved the principle in The Collector of Bombay v. Nusserwanji Rattanji Mistri; it disapproved the broader propositions in State of Madras v. A.Y.S. Parisutha Nadar.

issues.definition: In a statutory acquisition proceeding, if the government has an interest in the land or a private interest is subject to a government restriction, the government may assert that right and compensation is limited to the outstanding private interest.
